title: How would you design retry behavior without creating a retry storm?
description: Use exponential backoff, jitter, circuit breakers, and rate limiting to make retries safe and self-throttling.

data.text: A retry storm is what happens when many clients retry a failing service simultaneously. Instead of helping, the retries amplify the failure: the service receives a sudden wave of duplicate requests that it cannot handle, causing more failures and more retries. The system enters a positive feedback loop and can take down adjacent services too.

The interviewer is testing whether you understand retries as a system-level concern, not just a try-catch block. Safe retry design requires coordination across clients, middleware, and the failing service itself.

items: Exponential backoff: each retry waits longer than the previous one. A typical sequence is 1s, 2s, 4s, 8s, giving the service time to recover.
Jitter: add randomness to the delay so that thousands of clients do not retry on the same interval. Even a small jitter (±20%) dramatically reduces synchronized waves.
Retry budgets: cap the total retry rate per client or per route so retries cannot exceed a safe fraction of normal traffic.
Circuit breaker: stop retrying entirely after a threshold of failures and wait for a cooldown period before probing again.

data.text: The jitter splits clients across different retry times. Instead of 10,000 clients retrying at exactly 2 seconds, they spread across a window. This prevents synchronized waves that characterize retry storms.

A circuit breaker tracks recent failures. When failures exceed a threshold, the breaker opens and all calls fail immediately without reaching the service. After a cooldown period, the breaker enters a half-open state and allows one probe request. If it succeeds, the breaker closes; if it fails, the cooldown restarts.

data.text: Clients are not the only line of defense. The service itself should implement rate limiting and request coalescing. When many identical requests arrive during a retry storm, coalesce them into a single backend call and share the result across all waiters.

items: Rate limiting: cap the maximum request rate per client identity or API key.
Request coalescing: if 500 clients request the same uncached resource, make one backend call and fan out the response.
Graceful degradation: return a cached or simplified response instead of failing outright when under pressure.
Load shedding: reject requests with 503 before the service thread pool exhausts, preserving capacity for healthy requests.

data.title: Server-sent timeouts are your friend
data.text: If your service sets a 5-second HTTP timeout, clients that receive a 504 should not retry for 30 seconds — they should retry after the timeout plus jitter. Retrying before the original request has truly timed out wastes resources.

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: Always pair exponential backoff with jitter to prevent synchronized retry waves.
Use circuit breakers to stop hammering a service that is clearly struggling.
Implement server-side rate limiting and request coalescing to absorb retry storms.
Retry budgets and server timeouts work together to keep retry rates within safe bounds.
data.takeaway: Retries should be conservative, self-throttling, and coordinated between client and server.
